substitution_note: Spec-named source: GDELT's raw event and mention streams (CAMEO-coded 15-minute CSVs at data.gdeltproject.org/gdeltv2/; ~52,000 files across this 24-month window). Actually used: the GDELT DOC 2.0 API (api.gdeltproject.org/api/v2/doc/doc, mode=timelinevolraw to locate coverage then mode=artlist to retrieve it), article-level, queried per obligor with GDELT's tone<-5 filter, carrying the same 15-minute seendate granularity as the raw stream. Cost of the substitution: GDELT's own CAMEO entity tagging is NOT used here — matching is by name query against a search string, which is lossy in the same way the WARN employer-name join is lossy, and near-duplicate articles across adjacent time slices (same title, different seendate) are real GDELT behaviour, kept as distinct mentions rather than silently merged. A second, narrower cost: `mode=artlist` does not return a per-article tone score (confirmed live — the payload carries only url/url_mobile/title/seendate/socialimage/domain/language/sourcecountry). Every mention here passed the server-side tone<-5 filter, so its true tone is below -5, but the `tone` field records that threshold string rather than a fabricated per-article number. A third cost, found and fixed during build: quoting the RAW Postgres `legal_name` verbatim (e.g. EDGAR's registrant-index form "CHARTER COMMUNICATIONS, INC. /MO/") produces an unmatchable literal phrase and silently returns zero results — indistinguishable from genuine "no adverse coverage". Each row's `employer_query` field carries the original legal_name (provenance); `gdelt_query` carries the exact query string sent to the API, built from the normalised name (state-suffix and trailing legal-form words stripped, e.g. "Charter Communications"). Words that are often part of the real public-facing name — Group, Holdings, Trust, Partners, Brands, REIT — are deliberately NOT stripped, so a handful of obligors whose media-common name drops one of those (e.g. "Vertiv" for "Vertiv Holdings Co") still search under the fuller form and may under-recall. A fourth cost, also found during build: GDELT rejects a quoted phrase below a minimum length with HTTP 200 and the plain-text body "The specified phrase is too short." — another silently-empty result if unhandled. One obligor is affected (XPO, Inc. -> "XPO"); its query falls back to the UNQUOTED term, which GDELT matches more loosely than an exact phrase. Its rows are therefore lower-precision than the rest, and `gdelt_query` shows the unquoted form so that is visible per row rather than hidden. A fifth cost, the largest: the DOC API silently truncates a long date range. Asked for the full 24 months it scans backwards from enddatetime, returns only the trailing ~3 months, and stops short of maxrecords — so nothing about the response says it was cut. Measured: "TUPPERWARE BRANDS" over the full window returns 0 articles; the same query over 2024-09..2024-11 returns 71, its Chapter 11 coverage. The DOC API's timeline modes are NOT clamped, so this sweep queries mode=timelinevolraw first for each obligor (one call, daily buckets across all 24 months), then issues mode=artlist calls only over the day ranges that carry volume, each sized to stay under the 90-day span limit and the 250-record cap. The timeline's summed counts are retained per obligor under `coverage` as the EXPECTED article total, so the retrieved rows can be checked against a figure the API itself supplied rather than being accepted because they arrived; in the run that produced this artifact the two agreed to within one article in 952. Coverage is the full 24-month window: mentions run 2024-08-19 to 2026-08-14, 353 of them in 2024, 329 in 2025 and 269 in 2026. A sixth cost, and the one a consumer of this file is most likely to be burned by: matching by name means an obligor whose short name is also a place, a person or an ordinary word collects adverse coverage that has nothing to do with it. A sampling review of the first full sweep found "Regis" (898 mentions, 0 of 25 sampled genuine — Bognor Regis and Lyme Regis court reports, an Australian gold miner, St. Regis hotels), "Sabre" (756, 0 of 25 — a professional wrestler and the idiom "sabre-rattling") and "Griffon" (155, 0 of 155 — a vulture and a radio host). Those 1,809 rows, 66% of the original artifact, were REMOVED: each of those three obligors was re-queried under its qualified corporate name, every qualified form measured returns zero articles across the window, and that fetched zero replaced the noise. "Celanese" was reviewed and RETAINED at 49 rows despite 25 of them being police blotters from Celanese, Texas and Celanese Road in Rock Hill, South Carolina, because the rest is genuine chemical-industry coverage that the qualified form would discard. Findings are recorded per obligor under coverage[lei].precision_review, whose `recommended_use` field is the one to branch on; an obligor with no precision_review entry was not reviewed, which is not the same as having been reviewed and passed.

precision_review.finding: The wrestler Zack Sabre Jr., and the idiom 'sabre-rattling'. Sabre Corp and Sabre Corporation both return zero across the window.
The griffon vulture in Spanish and French wildlife press, and a radio host named Moon Griffon. Griffon Corp and Griffon Corporation both return zero.

Bognor Regis, Lyme Regis and Rowley Regis court and crime reports; Regis Resources, an Australian gold miner; St. Regis hotels. Every qualified form measured (Regis Corp, Regis Corporation, Regis Salons) returns zero articles across the window, so the 898 rows were replaced by a fetched zero rather than corrected.

'Celanese' is a place as well as a company — Celanese, Texas is a company town named after the corporation, and Celanese Road runs through Rock Hill, South Carolina. 25 of 49 titles are police blotters and local crime reports from those two places, affirmatively about something other than the company. The remainder is genuine chemical-industry coverage (the Clariant / LyondellBasell / Dow ethylene damages suits, a plant acid spill, Texas freeze shutdowns). Not replaced: unlike Regis, Sabre and Griffon the qualified form is not empty — 'Celanese Corp' returns 4 articles — but swapping 49 mixed rows for 4 clean ones would discard real industry coverage to buy a precision number. Flagged for down-weighting instead, so the choice is the consumer's.
